Now, let us discuss morphisms from spectra of fields.
Let <MATH_0001> be a local ring
with maximal ideal <MATH_0002> and residue field <MATH_0003>.
Let <MATH_0004> be a field. A local homomorphism <MATH_0005> by definition
factors as <MATH_0006>, i.e., is the same thing as
a morphism <MATH_0007>. Thus we see that morphisms
<MATH_0008>
correspond to pairs <MATH_0009>. We may define
a preorder on morphisms of spectra of fields to <MATH_0010>
by saying that <MATH_0011> dominates
<MATH_0012> if <MATH_0013>
factors through <MATH_0014>. This suggests
the following notion: Let us temporarily
say that two morphisms <MATH_0015> and
<MATH_0016> are <TEXTITOPEN_0001>equivalent<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if there exists
a third field <MATH_0017> and a commutative diagram
<MATH_0018>
Of course this immediately implies that the unique points of
all three of the schemes <MATH_0019>,
<MATH_0020>, and <MATH_0021>
map to the same <MATH_0022>. Thus a diagram (by the remarks above)
corresponds to a point <MATH_0023> and a commutative diagram
<MATH_0024>
of fields. This defines an equivalence relation, because given
any set of field extensions <MATH_0025> there exists
some field extension <MATH_0026> such that all
the field extensions <MATH_0027> are contained in the extension <MATH_0028>.
